title: Word order: two simple rules
summary: The engine goes last, and anything that describes something goes before it. Particles do the rest of the work.

blocks.text: You will hear two claims about Japanese word order: "it is subject-object-verb" and "order does not matter". Both come from asking European questions about Japanese. Mary-hit-Susan can be メアリーがスーザンをなぐった or スーザンをメアリーがなぐった. Who did what to whom is decided by **が** and **を**, not by position. Yet order does matter in two other places.
Whatever the engine is (a verb, an い-adjective, or a noun plus だ / です), it closes the logical sentence. A few sentence-ending particles such as ね may follow, but the engine is the true end.
Rule 2: a describer goes before what it describes

Anything that modifies a thing (a noun) must stand in front of it: a blue dress, the dress I bought at the market. Japanese never wraps a clause on the other side, as English does with "the dress **I bought**". So you always read in the same direction.
Take a full clause and move one piece to the engine end: it stops being a sentence and becomes a describer for that piece.

cars.label: the dress I bought at the market

blocks.text: 市場で買ったドレス。 The dress (I) bought at the market.

How do you know whether something is a full sentence or a describer? Look at the end. If it ends in an engine, it is a logical clause. If it ends in a noun, that noun is the thing being described by everything in front of it.

blocks.jp: 市場で買ったドレスを友達にあげた。
blocks.en: (I) gave my friend the dress I bought at the market.

blocks.jp: ドレスを買った市場は駅の近くだ。
blocks.en: The market where (I) bought the dress is near the station.

blocks.jp: 赤い帽子をかぶっている少女が笑った。
blocks.en: The girl wearing a red hat laughed.

items: **Rule 1:** the engine (verb, adjective or noun + copula) goes at the end.
**Rule 2:** anything that modifies a noun goes before it.
**が** and **を** show who and what; position does not.
A clause that ends in a noun is a describer, not a sentence.

questions.prompt: Japanese word order never matters, because you can put words in any order.
questions.note: It matters for the engine position and for modifiers; only the が/を order is flexible.

questions.instruction: Both sentences say the same. What tells you who hit whom?
questions.prompt: メアリーがスーザンをなぐった / スーザンをメアリーがなぐった
questions.note: が marks who did it, を marks what it was done to.
In 昨日読んだ本 the noun at the end is described by 昨日読んだ.
The clause 妹が作った describes ケーキ.

questions.instruction: Which is a complete logical clause?
questions.note: It ends in an engine; the others end in a noun.

questions.instruction: Make the noun "the market" the modified noun
questions.prompt: （私が）市場でドレスを買った。
options: 市場でドレスの買った
questions.note: Move 市場 to the engine end and drop its で.

questions.prompt: the dress that my mother bought
questions.note: The clause comes first and the noun it describes comes last.

questions.prompt: (I) ate the cake my brother baked.
questions.note: 弟が焼いた describes ケーキ; the engine 食べた closes the sentence.

questions.instruction: Which is not allowed in Japanese?
options: The describer after its noun, as in "dress I bought"
A noun with a clause in front
questions.note: A describing clause always comes before the noun.

questions.instruction: A clause ends in a noun. What does that tell you?
options: It is a describer for that noun
It has no engine, but still counts as a sentence
questions.note: Only a clause ending in an engine is a logical clause.
